2.text: The story breaks off at this episode. It is probably only a fragment of

3.text: a fuller tale. The name Bony-Face is well known among story-tellers. They

4.text: say that he was one of the strongest warriors; but all tales in which his

5.text: name is mentioned are only short fragments. It is interesting to note that

6.text: this tale represents Head-Nodder as no great hero, and even gives him a

7.text: brother with the ridiculous name of Soft-Buttocks. The last name is formed

8.text: perhaps in contrast to the hard cheeks of Bony-Face. Bony-Face vanquished

9.text: them without difficulty at one time or another. Perhaps these tales are the

10.text: reminiscences of some ancient local rivalries, or else an attempt at parody of

11.text: the old traditions. In the parallel case of the Russian epic legends of ancient

12.text: warriors, these have given rise to the formation of certain parodies, which

14.text: Temeˊereč, or, in diminutive form, Temeereˊčeqäi, is a young man light

15.text: of foot and quick of motion. His parents were killed by Taˊn˙ñɪt, and he

17.text: “One time the Taˊn˙ñɪt made inroads on the Chukchee territory. The people fled, driving

18.text: with reindeer. The little boy was walking ahead. The first driver overtook him. ‘Take me with

19.text: you!’ — ‘Let the rear drivers take you.’ The rear drivers overtook him. ‘Take me with you!’ —

20.text: ‘Let the last ones take you.’ Then the very last one came to him. ‘Take me with you!’ — ‘No,

21.text: let them that are behind take you! — ‘Ah me! There is no one behind.’¹

22.text: “The last man went away, and the boy was left alone. He followed the tracks of the drivers.

23.text: A small boy he was, but a clever one. He carried in his hands a child’s bow and one arrow with

24.text: a copper head. The line of the pursuing Taˊn˙ñɪt was approaching from behind, the strongest

25.text: warrior was far ahead. The boy looked back and thought, ‘What shall I do?’ He ran and fell

26.text: down, jumped up and ran again. The Taˊn˙ñɪn warrior saw him running and jumped down from

27.text: the sledge. Then he took off his armor and put it on the sledge, and also the spear. The spear

28.text: was a very strong one. The handle was thicker than a man’s arm. He ran, leading the reindeer

29.text: by the bridle. The boy thought, ‘This one will crush me with his nail as he would a little louse.’

30.text: He looked back again. The Taˊn˙ñɪn warrior was getting nearer. In a few moments he would

31.text: overtake him. The fur shirt of the Taˊn˙ñɪn was very short: it hardly covered his abdomen. The

32.text: boy shot his bow and wounded him in the abdomen. The warrior sat down upon the snow.

33.text: ‘Stop, boy!’ said the warrior. ‘Come here!’ The boy was afraid to come. The Taˊn˙ñɪn stood up,

34.text: took the spear from the sledge, and put it on the ground. He also took off his armor and put it

35.text: down. ‘Come here! I will not hurt you. It is for your benefit.’ Then the boy came. ‘There, take

36.text: the bow and spear and armor. Put on all of it, take the sledge, and drive on. Do not be afraid

37.text: of our people. They will find my body and turn back, because I am the strongest.’²

38.text: “After that the boy came home and lived with his uncle. He was growing fast, and all the

39.text: time performing exercises. One time when the people arranged a reindeer-race, the young hero

40.text: offered to draw his uncle’s sledge, acting in place of a reindeer-buck. He prepared the sledge and

41.text: attached the traces and put on the breast-collar. Then he said to his uncle, ‘Put the bridle on

42.text: me!’ — ‘No need of it,’ said the uncle. ‘Go along!’ He rushed forward. ‘Wait, wait!’ cried his

43.text: uncle. ‘The sledge jolts too much.’ He put the bridle on the young man and took the reins.

45.text: “The trail was quite crooked. He said, ‘Let us go straight ahead!’ There was no trail. The

46.text: snow was knee-deep; but he ran on as if there were no snow.
